narrative.summary: Qatar governs AI mainly through strategy and voluntary guidance led by the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT); no AI-specific law has been identified so far. The National AI Strategy (2019) and the Digital Agenda 2030 set direction, and the Artificial Intelligence Committee, created by Council of Ministers Decision No. 10 of 2021, coordinates implementation. MCIT's companion principles and guidelines for ethical AI development and deployment and for ethical AI use (November 2024), and its AI Workplace and Job Transformation Guidelines (June 2026), form the soft-law core identified so far. Binding obligations identified so far come from the Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016), the Qatar Central Bank's AI Guideline (2024) for licensed financial institutions, and the QFC courts' 2026 practice direction on AI use in proceedings. The next step is a National AI Policy, put out for consultation in December 2025 and still listed by MCIT as upcoming in October 2026, which proposes a central AI policy unit and risk-based oversight of AI.
lead_institutions: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
Qatar International Court and Dispute Resolution Centre (QICDRC)
narrative.review_notes: Reviewed again on 18 October 2026 against the websites of the communications ministry, the Qatar Legal Portal (Al Meezan), the National Cyber Security Agency and the courts; the National AI Policy is still listed as upcoming and has not been adopted. The cyber security agency's February 2024 guidelines on secure AI use are listed under Leads because no official copy was found on its new website, and the effective date of the personal data law is still to be confirmed.

instruments.summary: Council of Ministers decision (11 articles) establishing the Artificial Intelligence Committee within the then Ministry of Transport and Communications, chaired by the ministry with the Qatar Computing Research Institute as vice-chair and members from ministries, universities and research and development bodies. Members serve renewable three-year terms. The committee sets mechanisms to implement Qatar's AI strategy and follows up on them, oversees government AI programmes and initiatives, recommends AI talent plans, supports AI start-ups and research, handles international cooperation and reports periodically on strategy implementation.

This is the document earlier listed separately as MCIT's 'AI Guidelines for Developers'; an undated earlier layout is hosted on the government asset store used by MCIT and Sharek.
instruments.summary: Voluntary guidance from MCIT for anyone developing or deploying AI systems that affect the public, aligned with UNESCO and OECD principles and Qatar National Vision 2030. It sets eight principles, from 'do no harm' backed by risk assessment, through robustness and security, avoiding bias and discrimination, environmental sustainability, privacy and transparency, to human accountability, each with practical guidelines. Users of AI are referred to a companion document on ethical use, and organisations are encouraged to adapt the guidance to their context.

instruments.issuing_authority: President of the Qatar International Court (QFC Civil and Commercial Court) and Chairman of the QFC Regulatory Tribunal
instruments.current_status: In force for proceedings before the QFC Court and the Regulatory Tribunal (QICDRC). Signed by Lord Thomas of Cwmgiedd (President of the Qatar International Court) and Sir William Blair (Chairman of the QFC Regulatory Tribunal), dated 6 January 2026; QICDRC news release of 06 January 2026 announces issue together with accompanying Practice Guidance. No separate commencement date is stated, so no commencement date is given. Issued after the contempt judgment in Jonathan David Sheppard v Jillion LLC [2025] QIC (E) 3. Classed mandatory-in-scope: binding on the QICDRC courts and their users only (PROTOCOL §3 court rule).
instruments.summary: Practice Direction issued under articles 38.2 and 26.2 of the Rules and Procedures of the QFC Civil and Commercial Court and the QFC Regulatory Tribunal, binding litigants, legal representatives and practitioners who use AI in proceedings. It makes Court Users responsible for verifying all AI-generated material and citations against primary sources, bars entering confidential or privileged information into AI tools except private secure platforms, prohibits using AI to generate or tamper with evidence, and requires disclosure of multimedia AI-generated or enhanced evidence. Pre-emptive declaration of AI use is not required unless the Court asks; misuse can lead to disregarded pleadings, adverse costs, referral to professional regulators or contempt proceedings.

instruments.current_status: Published by MCIT on its Guidelines page; the document is dated November 2024. Not legally binding.
instruments.summary: Voluntary MCIT guidance for all users of AI systems in Qatar, including government employees, private companies and SMEs, students and researchers, and the public. It sets principles for responsible use, such as ensuring individual and social well-being, taking accountability, understanding AI's capabilities and limitations, minimising bias, protecting personal and sensitive data and complying with relevant laws, and addresses risks such as deepfakes and hallucinations. It is the companion to MCIT's guidance for AI developers and deployers.

instruments.issuing_authority: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)

instruments.current_status: Version 1.0.0 (Ref. DIA-GUI-004) dated June 2026, published on MCIT's Guidelines page. Issued under Amiri Decision No. 57 of 2021 and Ministerial Decision No. 17 of 2024; non-binding.
instruments.summary: Non-binding MCIT guidelines for public and private sector organisations adopting AI, giving a human-centred, task-based framework for redesigning jobs and managing workforce change. They set out phases to redesign work, identifying which tasks can be AI-augmented and which should stay human-led, and to empower and upskill staff, and address risks such as task displacement, deskilling, over-reliance on automated outputs and unclear accountability. The public sector is asked to take a whole-of-government approach.
